original_query: How do I track a bill that has been passed out of committee? This is a general question about the U.S. House of Representatives, but for specifics I will use HR 1320 of the 119th U.S. Congress. This bill was introduced Feb 13, 2025 and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce. It passed out of committee on July 23, 2025. My question is, "Now what?" The standard answer is, "It goes to the full House for debate and a vote," but that answer is short on details for someone who's trying to keep track of a bill. This blog post , if accurate, has a few more details, most notably that the Speaker of the House will work with the House Rules Committee to place the bill on one of four calendars. For instance, the Union Calendar seems to the most common calendar. That appears to be available at govinfo.gov as a file that gets updated into a new file each day. Browsing through the most up-to-date one (Nov 10, linked above), I don't see any reference to HR 1320. I can conclude that in the three and a half months between when HR 1320 was passed from committee to today, the Speaker and the Rules Committee have not placed it on the Union Calendar to be debated and voted on. That's all I seem to be able to determine, though. Is there any way of knowing the status of this bill during this time? Is there any way of knowing when the Speaker and Rules Committee will place the bill on one of the calendars, and which calendar it will be? Do I have to download PDFs of all four calendars every day to check to see if the bill has been added to one?

turns.query: In Congress, what actually happens when a bill is 'ordered to be reported' by a committee, and how is that different from it being put on a calendar for debate?
turns.answer: When a bill is 'ordered to be reported' by a committee, it means the committee has finished reviewing it and is sending it to the full House for possible consideration. At that point, the bill gets placed on one of the House's calendars, which are basically lists of bills that could be brought up for debate. But just being on a calendar doesn't mean the bill will actually be debated or voted on—it just makes it eligible. Putting a bill on the calendar is different from scheduling it for debate, which is a separate step decided by House leadership and the Rules Committee.

original_query: In simple terms, what is the commonly accepted difference in meaning between "nation" and "state" in a political context? It is not infrequent that users post lengthy arguments and rebuttals based on their claims about finer points of nuances in meaning between those two words. Based on my knowledge of the general usage of both words, which exist in both English and French, they seem generally quite interchangeable, including in many political contexts . That duality also exists in Dutch, but I am too rusty at it to remember if there is much difference in usage. Point being that many Latin-influenced languages have both words and they seem to equivalent in many, not all, contexts * . And that includes official documents where both words appear together with little to distinguish them. When Louis XIV allegedly says "L'État, c'est moi " / "I am the state!" that phrase would be just as recognizable today as "I am the nation!". There is nothing wrong per se with specialized, specific, technical terms within a particular domain (at least when it doesn't veer into jargon which is not generally considered favorably). But when the general usage doesn't support much distinction, it seems to me people arguing on the basis of distinct meanings need to be much more explicit in what exactly supports their arguments. Pardon my veering into computer programming as an example... That field's extensive jargon allows for undifferentiated/equivalent use of both "arguments" and "parameters" when used in contexts like "I called this program with these arguments" vs. "I called this program with these parameters" . I've always considered them interchangeable in most of the time when calling a program or function but I've heard people say that's not the case. And indeed, upon looking up some definitions, there do seem to be some differences. But, and that my key point here, not in any way that a practitioner of the field would generally find very important. I blissfully forgot 5 minutes later and that hasn't made a bit of difference because it hardly ever matters. Note that a related notion of "by value" vs "by reference" has important distinctions that are expected to be understood by any competent programmer, so it's not just general sloppiness and imprecision, it's just that "arguments" and "parameters" are mostly used interchangeably by programmers in that context. In specialized cases, like compiler design (apologies again for the veering into a field specific example), those nuances in meaning may very well be understood and meaningful. But I would expect the more knowledgeable party to explain a bit on their basis of argumentation when asked by a programmer or even layman that doesn't operate in that subfield. However, when the context is how a system is configured, parameters is the appropriate term, not arguments . That's based on common usage in that field. So, pardon my lack of knowledge in the matter, but what do people mean when they say that "nation" is not the same thing as "state"? What are the commonly accepted sources for that distinction? Can you cite them? * Like my example about computer terminology above, this is not to say they are always synonymous. In a context of chauvinism, one will talk of nationalism . While statism will be more appropriate when discussing say economic management. If talking about bureaucracy, state is appropriate most of the time, not nation . National flags. State does have a particular meaning in the USA, but other countries use the word province or Länder to denote essentially the same notion of sub-national units and that looks like a different use of the word "state" entirely. You might say "nation-building", but "state-building" would be less common. Ethnicity considerations are a closer match to "nation". That's rather obvious from their day-to-day use and dictionary examples would support those distinctions. It's more good English usage (and good French usage, in more or less the same way). In other words, it is more dictated by usual terminology , rather than by deep semantic differences between the two words when they are both appropriate terms within a given context. On the notion of autonomous, self-governing, political entities with defined borders however, those two, along with the word "country" (might as well double down on sloppiness) seem roughly equivalent to me. And that is mostly what I am asking about here: educate me on the differences in that context
original_answer: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State State (polity), a centralized political organization that regulates law and society within a territory https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation A nation is a type of social organization where a collective identity, a national identity, has emerged from a combination of shared features across a given population, such as language, history, ethnicity, culture, territory, or society. Some nations are constructed around ethnicity (see ethnic nationalism) while others are bound by political constitutions (see civic nationalism ). So essentially the state is the government (not the people but the structural apparatus) of a place, while a nation is some sort of tribe (whether it's by family connections, by tradition, language, culture, heritage, values, contract or whatnot). Nowadays "nation states", so countries where a nation demands the ability to govern itself (and be that state) are somewhat the norm for modern countries, but that's actually rather novel. For example with Louis XIV and absolute monarchs in general, the government was quite distinct from the nation. And with colonialism and imperialism it was quite common to have a government and a population, where the population had no intrinsic political agency and didn't see or explicitly constituted itself as a tribe/nation, but where you have no common group, but more individuals or where you have several different groups within an empire which may or may not defined themselves as a nation. And those different groups may have existed as a nation way before they had a territory and the political control over said territory, so a nation without a state and a state without a nation.

It’s more about a shared identity and feeling of belonging than about actual borders or governments.

Q: How does the idea of sovereignty fit in when the nation and the state don’t really line up?

original_query: What violent acts or injuries are attributable to Palestine Action? The UK government has recently proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group. According to the Prime Minister's spokesperson (reported in The Express , The Guardian , The Independent , and other outlets; emphasis mine), We’ve said that many people may not yet know the reality of this organisation, but the assessments are very clear: this is a violent organisation that has committed violence, significant injury , extensive criminal damage, and as I say, it has met the tests as set out under the Terrorism Act to be proscribed. The words "violence" and especially "injuries" are generally understood to mean harm against people, not inanimate objects such as aircraft; and the listing of these separately from "criminal damage" suggests them as separate categories. However, at least on their Wikipedia page , it seems that Palestine Action's actions mainly involve property damage and trespass. The one exception I'm able to find is that three members (Ms Garland, Ms Hobson and Ms Kamal) were charged with one count of assault by beating, during an action in which they and another person reportedly broke windows and splashed red paint at an Elbit Systems facility; this was reported by BBC News , without further details of the alleged assault, which also was not mentioned by BBC News at the time of their arrest . On the other hand, the Prime Minister's spokesperson's statement alludes to acts which "people may not yet know", suggesting evidence against the group which has not yet been widely reported, but which people at least would have the opportunity to know about. The wording "may not yet know" would not quite be consistent with non-public information, as in that case the spokesperson should say that people don't yet know, rather than that they may not yet know. What violent acts or injuries have been undertaken or caused, or allegedly undertaken or caused, by Palestine Action? For the purposes of this question, "violent acts" and "injuries" mean those against people, not property. I'm interested in more details of the assault charge mentioned above, and any other instances.
original_answer: A good question, not least because much has been made out of Palestine Action being the only group apparently proscribed on the basis of property damage (albeit a lot of it). What violent acts or injuries are attributable to Palestine Action? In the sense of a legal fact, none (so far as I'm aware): while a number of alleged members of Palestine Action face charges related to violence, at the time of writing the only convictions relate to property damage. But: Italian Philosopher's answer mentions charges related to violence against people. In respect of those, as there are 'active proceedings' the British media (and everyone else in the UK) must take care when commenting on them (see Channel4's guidance on contempt ). A summary of the charges related to injury or violence (these links are to the law): aggravated burglary (burglary with a weapon or an article intended to be used as a weapon - 23 people are charged with this) assault by beating (statutory version of common law battery, a summary only offence, 3 charged with this) assault of an emergency worker (police officers - here it will be a sentence enhancer, not a standalone offence) actual bodily harm (need not be permanent but must be more than transient and trifling, 1 person faces two counts of this) grievous bodily harm (serious or permanent physical injury, one person charged with this, alleged victim is a police officer) violent disorder (three or more people use or threaten violence, and their combined actions would cause a reasonable person to fear for their safety - 18 people are charged with this) There are more than 20 defendants in total. Incident date Persons Charges News report date 6 August 2024 1 criminal damage, violent disorder, grievous bodily harm with intent, two counts of actual bodily harm, aggravated burglary 13 August 2024 6 August 2024 5 criminal damage, violent disorder, aggravated burglary 13 August 2024 (as above) 6 August 2024 1 criminal damage and aggravated burglary 13 August 2024 (as above) 6 August 2024 2 criminal damage, aggravated burglary 16 August 2024 6 August 2024 1 criminal damage, aggravated burglary, violent disorder 16 August 2024 (as above) 6 August 2024 6 aggravated burglary, criminal damage, violent disorder 23 November 2024 6 August 2024 2 aggravated burglary, criminal damage 23 November 2024 (as above) 15 March 2025 3 assault by beating, conspiracy to damage property 17 March 2025 15 March 2025 1 conspiracy to damage property 17 March 2025 (as above) 6 August 2024 5 aggravated burglary, criminal damage and violent disorder 19 July 2025 All the incidents dated 6 August 2024 are the same incident. Crown Prosecution Service guidance on offences against the person . Also, I don't necessarily agree 1 with the proscription 2 but I also think the attitude that "it's only property damage" may underestimate all the consequences of 'direct actions'. Imagine being an ordinary worker or customer in a high street bank and some bricks are thrown through the windows. It doesn't cause any injuries, it's only charged as criminal damage, but would it be unreasonable in the moment for an ordinary person to fear injury or violence? They don't know the intentions of the perpetrators, who could be anything from vandals to bank robbers. Face to face, if I were to intentionally or recklessly cause another person to fear immediate physical harm, I would be committing an assault. It is also an offence to intentionally or recklessly cause alarm or distress . 1 I do agree with the MPs who criticised the fact that the Government put Palestine Action along with another two organisations on one proscription order, which meant MPs could only abstain or vote for or against all three to be proscribed, they could not vote for or against each organisation individually. The other two organisations certainly do intend and plan mass injury and murder. Publicly available information does not suggest the same of Palestine Action. 2 The proscription of Palestine Action will be judicially reviewed in late 2025.

There is also some ambiguity as to what counts as a "leader" here: as such, I shall assume that anyone speaking clearly on behalf of a governing party or entity, such as a domestic spokesperson or international delegate, is conveying the position of the leader. Guyana is a mid-income nation in the Western hemisphere, specifically a continental Caribbean country, where English and an English-influenced creole language are the primary languages. For instance, California has 52 congressmen in the House, and would thus give each Senator 26 votes for initiating and sustaining a filibuster. No Senator gets fractional votes, and so Wyoming gets 1 vote per Senator. This is probably politically unpalatable, so I considered the idea of instituting a log base 2 rounded up Example state calculations: CA: log2(52) = 5.7 rounded up -> 6 votes per Senator. TX: log2(38) = 5.2 rounded up -> 6 votes per Senator. CT: log2(5) = 2.3 rounded up -> 3 votes per Senator. WY: log2(1) = 0, 0 would be handled by a special rule -> 1 vote per Senator. The key is to not let a majority of states fall below the threshold that every state is under now, as every state has 2 Senators out of 100, that threshold is 2%. Now, my formula would result in 288 votes, (just on filibusters) among the 50 states. Thus each state only needs 3 votes per senator to get 2.1% of the vote, a small improvement on 2%. To get 3 votes per Senator, you only need 5 reps as the CT calculation above proved. Connecticut is the smallest state with 5 house reps, and is the 29th largest state, thus a current Senate majority exists. original_answer: Question: Hypothetical: Hurdles to Weighting Votes on the Senate Filibuster Short Answer: The U.S. constitution doesn’t dictate or mention filibuster cloture. Article I, Section 5 gives each chamber of Congress the power to “determine the Rules of its Proceedings.” This means the Senate can decide for itself how debate works—how long it lasts, how it ends, and what vote thresholds are needed for different actions. The Constitution does specify supermajority requirements in only a few cases, such as: 2/3 vote to override a veto, 2/3 vote to ratify treaties, and 2/3 vote to expel a member. While changing the Senate cloture rule would not require a change to the U.S. Constitution it would require a change to the senate standing rules which while not as involved would be nearly as impossible even if one party held the necessary votes. Altering or "weighting" votes on the filibuster isn’t just a matter of policy preference, it’s a massive institutional challenge. It would require supermajority rule changes, overcoming deep partisan resistance, the super majority in the senate voting to reduce the influence and authority of most of its individual senators, navigating unpredictable public sentiment, and building entirely new systems for managing legislative power. One might persuade California, Texas, New York, and Florida; but why would the other 46 states support it? Answer: Meaning shifting how much power individual senators or their votes carry over the 60 vote threshold (for cloture). That’s not currently how the Senate works, and implementing such a change would face multiple significant hurdles, including constitutional, procedural, political, and practical obstacles. The filibuster and its cloture rule (formerly Rule XXII, now part of Senate standing rules) are internal Senate processes—not explicitly required by the Constitution but they’re considered legitimate Senate rules under Article I, §5. To change them, the Senate must adopt a new rule. However, Rule XXII itself requires a two-thirds vote to amend (on the first ballot), essentially needing ~67 votes supermajority agreement to even start changing how cloture works. Which would mean getting the supermajority support for reducing the power and influence of the very same super majority. Filibuster norms are deeply embedded in Senate culture as a minority protection: they allow a single 41-member minority to block most legislation, effectively giving each vote substantial weight. Any major modifications would upend a centuries‑old balance that safeguards against instant majoritarian policy swings. Various reform ideas are floating around. Lowering the cloture threshold gradually after failed cloture votes, reinstitute a "talking filibuster" (requiring a senator to continuously hold the floor), or creating issue‑specific exceptions (e.g., for voting rights, Supreme Court nominees); but each reform requires political consensus—and each risks setting precedents that could unravel the filibuster entirely. The nuclear option (simple‑majority rule change) has already been used twice—for judicial and executive nominations—but would be politically explosive if tried for legislation. Enforcing weighted voting could demand new bureaucratic structures, fairness metrics, and oversight—all hard to build and maintain in a highly partisan body. From comments: From Bobson Yes, it doesn't take an amendment to change the rules of cloture, but it does take an amendment to change the weighting of a vote. Or if the argument is that it doesn't, it should explain why. the Constitution DOES require: for final passage of a bill, ratification of treaties, and other constitutionally enumerated votes, each senator must have one vote, and every senator’s vote is counted equally. In those votes you can’t give one senator more votes than another when voting on the actual question of passing legislation, confirming nominations, etc. That would violate the principle of equal suffrage in the Senate. Cloture is different. A cloture vote is NOT the final vote on legislation, it’s just an internal procedural motion to end debate under the Senate’s own rules. Because it’s a procedural vote created entirely by Senate rules, the Senate could decide how to count it including weighting votes without violating the Constitution. In other words, cloture is not constitutionally mandated; it’s a creature of Senate rules. Changing how cloture is invoked would still leave the final passage vote equal. Think of senate committees. Not every senator even has a vote in committee only a small fraction of members do, but it doesn’t violate the constitution. It’s similar logic. Committees are governed by senate rules not the constitution and committees do not pass legislation only full equal votes in the senate chamber do that. Even though committees do vote on bills independently first it’s just a procedural vote governed by senate rules like cloture votes.

original_query: Is the sitting President of the United States meant to have representation in Congress as a U.S. citizen? The President of the United States retains the right to vote while holding office. Most US citizens live in an area where their ballot allows them to elect not just the President, but also a member of the House of Representatives and two (with staggered terms, so typically only one is on the ballot at any given time) members of the Senate. It stands to reason that the President wouldn't have a special ballot that only allows them to vote for their own office; that would be a different version of the right to vote than the rest of us have. So, given all of this, that suggests that a sitting President of the United States would likely also be a constituent of a U.S. Representative and two U.S. Senators. However, this is complicated by the fact that when elected, the President moves to the White House in Washington, D.C. D.C. does not have voting representation in Congress; they do elect a delegate to the House, but have no representation in the Senate. Voters who change address are required to update their voter registration with their new address if they want to remain registered to vote. This would suggest that every President has to update their voter registration as a resident of the District of Columbia (and is essentially the sum total of what I was told when I called USA.gov's answer line with this question). However, former President Biden went back to his home state of Delaware to cast his ballot in 2024. This would indicate that he remained registered in Delaware, which is not in itself illegal; registering in another state does not mean that your previous state is notified to take you off of its voter rolls. So if Biden voted in Delaware, he would have had a ballot for the district in the state where he is registered. This would presumably have included a House and Senate race, meaning he did in fact have a Representative and two Senators he could write to as a constituent. But if he had voted in D.C., he would have not been able to elect voting members of Congress. Where the President votes, then, materially changes their enfranchisement and who represents them in Congress; in other words, it matters. So the question then becomes where is the President supposed to vote: in their home state, or the territory of their primary residence (the White House), Washington, D.C.? Though a President can technically have representation in Congress by voting in their home state, is that really intentional?
original_answer: Short answer Is the sitting President of the United States meant to have representation in Congress as a U.S. citizen? Yes. U.S. citizens vote where they are domiciled. Your domicile is the place that you intend to be your permanent residence, in a manner not totally contradicted by your actions . A federal elected official's residence in the District of Columbia while serving in that office almost never constitutes a new domicile for that elected official (much like a member of the military who is in active military service is usually not domiciled for election purposes in the place where that member of the military is residing while deployed). The President generally votes in the place where the President was domiciled prior to assuming the Presidential office, which is generally the President's pre-election home address. As far as I know, no President has ever considered himself domiciled at the White House for purposes of voting in elections as a U.S. citizen. Members of Congress also invariably consider themselves to be domiciled in the state from which they were elected (as required by the U.S. Constitution as of the time that they are elected). This intent is reflected with respect to members of Congress in the U.S. Constitution, which states that members of House "when elected, be an Inhabitant of that State in which he shall be chosen." (but not necessarily in their Congressional District), U.S. Const. Art. I, § 2, and that Senators must also "when elected, be an Inhabitant of that State in which he shall be chosen", U.S. Const., Art I, § 3. In contrast, the President must be a natural born citizen who has "been fourteen Years a Resident within the United States." U.S. Const., Art. II,§ 1, but is not subject to any residency requirement in a particular state at the time that the President is elected (although Article II, Section 1 of the U.S. Constitution adopted in 1789, as modified by the 12th Amendment, adopted in 1804, effectively requires Presidential tickets in which the President and the Vice President are residents of different states at the time of their election). Thus, this is an intentional part of the design of Congress as it is currently structured. Does this matter? The representation in Congress that the President has as a U.S. citizen of some state, while intended, is trivial and immaterial. No President in U.S. history has made a meaningful attempt to appeal to this to gain influence in Congress, and no Presidential candidate's own vote has ever influenced whether that Presidential candidate won the Presidential election or not. Instead, Presidents have exerted influence in Congress through (1) a Vice President who can resolve tie votes in the Senate and has a right to preside over its proceedings if desired (once the constitution was amended to have the President and Vice President run on a single ticket following the adoption of the 12th Amendment in 1804), (2) the influence the President has as the leader of the Executive Branch with direct access to the resources of the federal government bureaucracy in matters like budget negotiations and Presidential nominations, (3) the influence the President has as the leader of his political party over the members of his party in Congress, and (4) sometimes the personal relationships that the President has developed with particular members of Congress from a lifetime in politics cumulating in being elected President. Since appropriations bills must originate in the House, where the President and Vice President both lack a voice and a vote, the President has to cultivate some ally in the House (often a leader in his party's caucus who serves on the appropriate House committee) to introduce his budget proposals. Nominations for political appointments, in contrast, and proposed treaties, can be submitted personally by the President, directly to the Senate, despite not being a Senator and not having to rely on the Vice President to do so, and these acts do not need to be approved by the House. Historical context But keep in mind that Senators were indirected elected by state legislatures until the adoption of the 17th Amendment in 1913. Until then, U.S. citizens did not directly vote for a U.S. Senator, only for their members of the state legislature. Similarly, members of the House were sometimes elected as a slate at the state level, or from several multimember districts, rather than from single member districts as they are today (and have been since the election of 1970), pursuant to a statute adopted in the 1967, now codified at 2 U.S.C. §2c , which was adopted as part of the civil rights movement to give black voters a greater say in electing members of Congress which multimember districts could suppress with the partisan winner-takes-all tendencies of an at large election from a multi-member district. So, many people were represented by multiple representatives in the U.S. House prior to 1970. And, of course, prior to the adoption of the 23rd Amendment in 1961, the District of Columbia has no say whatsoever in federal elections, and even now, the District of Columbia does not elect voting members of the House or Senate and only has a vote in Presidential elections, despite having a larger population than the least populous state (Wyoming), a fact not unrelated to the fact that the District of Columbia is majority black and unwaveringly supports Democrats by overwhelming majorities in all of its elections, which has led to Republican opposition to a constitutional amendment to change this or to granting statehood to the District of Columbia. For roughly a century before the 1960s, the politics of D.C. representation in the federal government were the same, but the party labels were reversed, with the Democratic party based in the "solid South" as the conservative anti-civil rights party, and the Republicans as the liberal leaning northern party, although this was muddled by dominant party Democratic government under FDR and Truman during the Great Depression and World War II. Also, keep in mind that prior to the U.S. Civil War, the federal government was a skeletal institution with much less power than state governments, from which members of Congress and federal judges below the U.S. Supreme Court level routinely resigned midterm to take more prestigious positions in state governments or the private sector, and was operated with much less professionalism than the modern federal government. The prestige of federal office prior to the U.S. Civil War was more akin to the prestige of holding an office in the European Union government or in the United Nations, today, compared to the prestige of holding a high office in the national government of an E.U. or U.N. member nation respectively. The power and importance of the federal government waned again not long after the Civil War, but started to grow again in the years leading up to World War I, and then grew much more during the New Deal during the Great Depression followed by World War II, to something much more like its current level of power and prestige, and with a much higher standard of formality and professinalism. The adoption of the 17th Amendment in 1913 was driven by the increasing importance that selection of U.S. Senators was having on elections to state legislatures as the federal government's power and prestige grew. The adoption of the 16th Amendment, formally authorizing the income tax, in 1913, also reflects this trend as the U.S. shifted from being funded primarily by tariff revenue to receiving a more stable and broad income tax base, that allowed it to fund a larger military and a bigger federal bureaucracy.

turns.answer: When it comes to voting for President and Vice President, if someone—like a sitting President—moves to a new state less than 30 days before the election and doesn’t meet the new state’s registration rules, they can still vote in their previous state. They can do this either in person or by absentee ballot, as long as they met the voting requirements in that previous state before moving.

original_query: What is the difference between a minority government and a coalition government? Canada's April 2025 national election was held yesterday, and it is currently looking likely that the Liberal Party will win a plurality, but not a majority, of seats in Canada's House of Commons. News reports suggest that if that does happen, that the Liberal Party will form a "minority government." In addition to the Conservative Party, which has little in common with the Liberal Party and will almost surely be the official opposition party after receiving the second largest number of seats in the House of Commons, there are three other political parties that won seats in the House of Commons: the Bloc Québécois, the New Democrat Party, and the Green Party. Depending upon the final vote counting results, the Liberal Party, together with one or two of these smaller parties, would have a 172 seat majority of the 343 seats in the House of Commons. And, none of the three smaller parties are so diametrically opposed to the agenda of the Liberal Party that finding common cause would be impossible. In many countries with parliamentary systems, when no one political party secures a majority of the seats in parliament, two or more political parties usually form a coalition government, in which cabinet seats are allocated among the coalition partners (usually in rough proportion to their numbers with the larger party getting the most important posts, but also based upon their legislative priorities), and the coalition develops a shared legislative agenda that gives every coalition member something that it wants and doesn't badly alienate any party in the coalition. This doesn't seem to be how a minority government works, but I'm not clear on that point, and none of the news accounts that I've seen explain in detail how it works. How does a minority government differ from a coalition government in a parliamentary system, and why is it assumed in Canada that there will be a minority government rather than a coalition government? The Canadian election prompted this question, but answers relevant to any parliamentary system of government would be appreciated. This question is not limited to this particular election, so it isn't moot, even if the Liberal Party ends up winning 172 seats or more in this election.
original_answer: One possible flavor of this arrangement is explained, about Canada, from September 2024, when the NDP's Singh pulled out of the minority deal with the Liberals (due to a dispute about dealing with a train strike). Canada's NDP pulls support for Trudeau's Liberals Canada’s left-wing New Democratic Party (NDP) has pulled the plug on a two-and-a-half-year-old agreement with Justin Trudeau's Liberals that had helped keep his minority government in power. The deal - called a "supply and confidence" agreement - had the NDP supporting the Liberals in confidence votes. In a statement released on Wednesday, Mr Singh said a non-confidence vote would be "on the table" with every confidence measure. Mr Trudeau and Mr Singh reached the agreement in March 2022, with the Liberals pledging to support the NDP on several of the party's key priorities in parliament. The deal differed to a coalition, where parties share power. Instead, the Liberals - who failed to win a majority in the past two elections - governed as a minority, but with assurances the NDP would support them in confidence votes. In exchange, Mr Singh's party secured progress on key priorities, including dental benefits for lower-income families and a national pharmacare programme covering birth control and insulin. From the wikipedia linked above, confidence and supply are, respectively: when the government is facing a motion of no-confidence and would be booted if it lost during the passing of budgets as not getting those done is essentially like losing a no-confidence vote. In parliamentary democracies based on the Westminster system, confidence and supply is an arrangement under which a minority government (one which does not control a majority in the legislature) receives the support of one or more parties or independent MPs on confidence votes and the state budget ("supply"). On issues other than those outlined in the confidence and supply agreement, non-government partners to the agreement are not bound to support the government on any given piece of legislation. 1 A coalition government is a more formal arrangement than a confidence-and-supply agreement, in that members from junior parties (i.e., parties other than the largest) gain positions in the cabinet and ministerial roles, and are generally expected to hold the government whip on passing legislation. Why not do this in return for cabinet positions/being part of the government/having a formal say on policy? Forming a formal coalition, as a very junior member, with a more dominant partner out of your ideological comfort zone may carry risks. I have several times read that the UK's Liberal Democrats made out badly from their 2010 coalition with the Conservatives because they held limited sway and got blamed by voters for Conservative goofs. Also, in Canada, you don't need any arrangements at all to run a minority government. (from a comment) It's also possible to continue to govern as a minority without any kind of agreement. All you have to do is make sure that for every measure you propose that might result in loss of confidence at least one of the other parties (with enough seats) supports the measure, or at least does not want to trigger an election. A good example of this would be Harper (Conservative) 2006 and Harper 2008 . This was a government with sizable support from voters, but well short of a majority and quite disliked by the other parties (can't remember what BQ's stance was however). Looking at Federal minority governments in Canada - Wikipedia , we see two things: many solo minority governments last only a short while. But some last 1-2 years. And agreed-upon support, like that in the NDP-Liberals deal I gave as an example, are the exception, rather than the rule. So most minority governments seem to be go-alone efforts to an extent: no coalition, no formal supply & confidence arrangement. Although this list may not fully document all informal quid-pro-quos entered into between parties (I won't attack you if you back my pet projects). This was kinda informally the case between the Liberals and the BQ after the NDP withdrawal in 2024: BQ (which can't win nationally anyway) would not cause problems for the Liberals as long as Quebec got treated nicely. Remember, in the absence of majority, who gets to form the government is whoever is invited to do so by the Governor General, i.e. presumably whoever the GG thinks is best suited to run a stable government. A comment indicates doubts about, stating that the opposition could topple the government relatively easily. True, but the opposition may not want to chance it unless the circumstances have changed substantially since the last election: voters may very well punish whoever triggers pointless elections. (FWIW: that was yet another peeve voters had against Trudeau: calling an election in 2021, during COVID, soon after 2019's, only due to thinking he'd do better). Of course, the best positioned opposition party (not necessarily the Official Opposition) wouldn't do the government any favors. But they'd probably only pull the trigger if could they expect a significant improvement from their previous performance. In fact, this effect is what happened with Harper 2011: minority => no confidence => election => majority. Last, but not least. Keep in mind that inter-party dynamics will play differently in Canada, with a first past the post system, 2-3 main parties + a regionally bounded BQ. Than it would in democracies with proportional representation and/or more highly fragmented parliaments where coalitions would be more necessary.

turns.query: In parliamentary governments, what’s the real difference between how smaller parties get cabinet roles in a coalition versus a minority government?
turns.answer: In a coalition government, smaller parties actually get a spot in the cabinet, meaning their leaders become ministers and help run the government directly. In a minority government, smaller parties might have a lot of influence over decisions and laws, but they don’t usually get cabinet roles—they just support or oppose the government from outside, sometimes in exchange for policy changes.

turns.query: What actually happens day-to-day if the government doesn’t have any official deals with the other parties?
turns.answer: If the government doesn’t have any official deals with other parties, things get a bit unpredictable day-to-day. They have to negotiate support for each bill or decision, meaning they might have to adjust their plans or make compromises to get enough votes. Opposition parties can have a lot of influence, because at any point they could team up and bring down the government with a confidence vote. This setup makes things less stable and forces the government to be flexible and responsive to other parties’ demands.

original_query: Did the Anti-Defamation League conflate protesting government actions with antisemitism in their 2024 audit? (re. CNN/Ryan Enos interview) In CNN's April 24, 2025 video Harvard's lawsuit against the Trump admin sets up a titanic clash over academic freedom after about 04:04, is this exchange between CNN and Prof. Ryan Enos (and website ) of Harvard's Department of Government. Transcript extracted via Python's youtube-transcript-api and lightly edited for broken/missing words and punctuation. CNN: [...] but the Anti-Defamation League, which I note has expressed concern about potential overreach by the administration, says antisemitic incidents hit a record high last year in their annual audit that's out today, and that it was fueled in part by campus protests. They have Massachusetts as number four nationally for antisemitic incidents, they have Boston and Cambridge as the hotspots in Massachusetts, and I know that you told my colleague Jessica Dean this weekend that Harvard has done enough to protect jewish students on campus; obviously you're open to them doing more. But I wonder what you think they should be doing if this deserves further action. ENOS: So I believe that any type of bigotry deserves action, and I want to make that crystal clear. But I would challenge the Anti-Defamation League or anybody else to make very clear as well that they can separate constitutional rights, especially ones that come to protest government action, like students protesting the United States support for Israel and its war on Gaza, from antisemitism. And if we start conflating those two things, then we are in very dangerous ground, because people in the United States have an absolute right to protest government action, and that does not make something antisemitic. And if you look at what the Anti-Defamation League has claimed, most of those incidents that the are incidences of people protesting the war, and that is clearly not antisemitism. And in fact, it's something that we should welcome in this country, because we believe in dissent, on college campuses or anywhere else. CNN: I do want to note; I think they tried to be very careful about not conflating those... Question: Did the Anti-Defamation League conflate protesting government actions with antisemitism in their 2024 audit ? (re. CNN/Ryan Enos interview)
original_answer: Arguably yes (but!) Many incidents had to do with Israel, and some were not necessarily anti-Semitic... Enos claims that most of the instances recorded by the Anti-Defamation League are people protesting the Israeli invasion of Gaza, and in a broad sense, this is probably almost true. The ADL writes in its report : More than half of all antisemitic vandalism incidents included references to Israel or Zionism. This is out of 2,606 incidents overall. And it also notes that 2,596 out of 6,552 incidents of harassment were at anti-Israel rallies (not quite a majority, but not too far off). Finally, it points out that: For the first time in the history of the Audit, a majority (58%) of all incidents contained elements related to Israel or Zionism. While I don't think that every incident that contained "elements related to Israel or Zionism" could be classified as a protest against the invasion of Gaza, I suspect that a large majority of them could be considered as such. Some of these incidents, to my judgment , could not be judged as facially anti-Semitic, even though they may have been motivated by anti-Semitism and may have been unpleasant for other reasons. For instance, the ADL writes: Activity at or surrounding anti-Israel protests frequently crossed the line into antisemitism through a range of concerning expressions. Protesters displayed justification or glorification of antisemitic violence, framing terror attacks against Israel and the Jewish community as justified "resistance," while others openly displayed support for U.S.-designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) by wearing Hamas headbands and waving Hezbollah and Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) flags. Protesters celebrated the anniversary of Hamas’s antisemitic October 7, 2023, terror attack on Israel and glorified the terrorist group leaders who masterminded the attack. Many protests featured rhetoric widely interpreted as a call to destroy Israel through slogans like "Death to Israel" or "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," alongside rhetoric explicitly marginalizing Jews with a connection to Israel, such as, "We don't want no Zionists here." Supporting Hamas's attacks against Israeli civilians might be morally wrong and in terrible taste, and it might be correlated with anti-Semitism, but it's difficult to say that it represents anti-Semitism a priori . For instance, some Palestinians may support Hamas because they see it as a choice between Hamas or annihilation by the IDF, while some non-Palestinians may simply not know anything about Hamas's anti-Semitic history. Some people saying, e.g. "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free" might be calling for the expulsion or killing of Jews, but others claim to view this "freedom" as meaning a plurinational state (the so-called one-state solution). Some people absolutely use "Zionist" as code for Jews (just look at David Duke and the Daily Stormer for some obvious examples). While this may make it a less-than-ideal term, this does not mean that everyone expressing their dislike for "Zionists" (e.g. "we don't want no Zionists here") is using it to refer to Jews, which the ADL seems to somewhat recognize, claiming that it is marginalizing people with "a connection to Israel." Plenty of people claim to use it to refer to what might be termed "Jewish nationalism." Such expressions may reasonably arouse suspicion of what else people might think, granted. But an audit of anti-Semitic incidents should require more than suspicion about people's motivations. In fact, the ADL used to agree with that statement! In the report, the organization admits that it changed its methodology after Hamas's attack on Israel in 2023, and that it previously did not count such incidents in its listing of anti-Semitism (not, at least, without other elements): Since October 7, 2023, ADL began to include in the Audit certain expressions of opposition to Zionism, as well as support for violent resistance against Israel or Zionists that could be perceived as supporting terrorism or attacks on Jews, Israelis or Zionists. It also notes: When they occur during public activism (such as at protests), in confrontations between individuals or in the form of vandalism (such as graffiti), these expressions constitute an implicit attack on the great majority of American Jews who view a relationship with Israel to be an integral part of their religious, cultural and/or social identities. Such rhetoric can be traumatizing to many American Jews and has led to their exclusion from some spaces simply because of that element of how they define and express their Jewishness. The ADL has been accused of taking a somewhat politicized stance in recent years, as when it absolved Elon Musk, a close ally of the Trump administration, of any responsibility for his alleged Nazi salute , and this may account for the broadening of its definitions. ...but some of the "anti-war" incidents were probably also anti-Semitic Enos comes very close to making the following syllogism: if an incident involved a protest against the Israeli invasion of Gaza, then it could not have been anti-Semitic: [...]most of those incidents that the are incidences of people protesting the war, and that is clearly not antisemitism[...] That implication is not clear, however. Someone could protest the Gaza war, but at the same time, include other elements that were anti-Semitic, and some of the examples that the ADL gives (to the extent that they are accurately representing them and to my judgment ), fall into that category. For instance, one incident occurred at a protest at a synagogue in New Jersey where attendees were celebrating the Israeli group ZAKA . This is pretty clearly an anti-war protest. However, one or more attendees apparently told the American Jews who were in attendance to "go back to Europe." Telling a group perceived as "foreign" to "go back to your country" is pretty classic bigotry, and when applied to Jews, could reasonably be called anti-Semitic. Similarly, they also claim: "At DePaul University, one individual was told, 'Go back to Poland,' near the encampment. Another individual was harassed by someone who stated they hoped they would be beheaded and that '[you] and the Jewish people like [you] should leave America.' " Another case that they mention involved someone who was shouting "Free Palestine" outside a Chabad in New York. By itself, not a priori anti-Semitic, if they knew that the Chabad had a pro-Israeli-government stance. Stabbing an Orthodox (and thus visibly) Jewish man who approached them...probably less so. I think this illustrates the basic idea that some of the instances recorded as being related to anti-war protests may also have actually been anti-Semitic incidents, a possibility that Enos does not seem to consider. As a side note, it is also important here to address a misconception here, one that seems to be implicit in what Enos says, and explicit in Trump's statements and actions: that if someone actually says something anti-Semitic, that action is not subject to the protection of the First Amendment. Enos says: But I would challenge the Anti-Defamation League or anybody else to make very clear as well that they can separate constitutional rights, especially ones that come to protest government action, like students protesting the United States support for Israel and its war on Gaza, from antisemitism. However, unlike in some jurisdictions (Germany or the U.K., for instance), the prevailing jurisprudence in the USA does not exclude anti-Semitic expression or other types of hate speech from constitutional protection. The current standard is the imminent lawless action test , which allows for government prohibition of only that speech that tends to clearly and foreseeably cause criminal action in the near future (and is intended to do so). As such, it would not be illegal for someone to say even "I hate all Jews, they should die." What might be subject to criminal penalties, on the other hand, would be if someone shouted "kill the Jews" in a crowd, some of which then proceeded to kill a Jew that they saw shortly thereafter.

turns.answer: The ADL doesn’t automatically call anti-Israel protests antisemitic. Only when the protest crosses a line, such as using slurs, promoting conspiracy theories, or calling for the destruction of Israel, does the ADL include it in their tally of antisemitic incidents.

Out of more than 5,000 anti-Israel rallies tracked in 2024, the ADL found that about half—2,596—had antisemitic messaging, like certain chants, signs, or speeches. They also talked about how tricky this can be and said they’re careful not to count regular protest activity as antisemitic unless it clearly crosses the line, so they really try to separate criticism of Israel from actual antisemitism when doing their audit.
turns.subquestion_reasoning: Select documents that detail the ADL's 2024 audit criteria or data on protest-related incidents and their classification as antisemitic, and avoid those lacking discussion of the protest vs. antisemitism distinction.

subquestion_reasoning_metadata.target_information: Documents should contain ADL's 2024 audit data or discussion on how anti-Israel protest incidents are classified as antisemitic, and any analysis of the distinction or overlap between protest and antisemitism.
relevance_signals: discussion of distinguishing protest from antisemitism

turns.conversation_history:
Q: In the ADL's 2024 audit, how did they decide what counts as antisemitism, especially when it comes to protests against Israel?
A: The ADL doesn’t automatically call anti-Israel protests antisemitic. Instead, they look for specific signs of antisemitism at these rallies—like hateful language, classic antisemitic stereotypes, or calls for violence against Jews or Israel. If a protest just criticizes Israeli policies or supports Palestinian rights, that isn’t counted as antisemitism in their audit. Only when the protest crosses a line, such as using slurs, promoting conspiracy theories, or calling for the destruction of Israel, does the ADL include it in their tally of antisemitic incidents.
Q: Would showing certain symbols at a protest automatically count as antisemitism, or is it more about the context?
A: It’s not just the symbol itself that automatically counts as antisemitism—it really depends on the context and how it’s being used. For example, the ADL does track all swastika incidents because of their strong association with the Holocaust and the trauma they cause for Jewish people. But for other symbols or slogans at protests, they look at the bigger picture: if the message crosses into antisemitic territory—like using classic stereotypes, calling for violence, or targeting Jewish institutions—then it’s counted as antisemitism. Simply showing a symbol isn’t always enough; it’s about what’s being said or implied and where it’s directed.
Q: Did they actually call out stuff like telling Jews to 'go back to Europe' as antisemitic, or did they separate that from just regular protest chants?
A: Yes, the ADL does count things like telling Jews to “go back to Europe” as antisemitic, not just as regular protest chants. They’re clear that they only include protest activity in their audit if it crosses a line into antisemitism—like using classic antisemitic slurs, stereotypes, or targeting Jews as a group. So, chants or comments that single out Jews or use hateful language definitely get included as antisemitic incidents, not just as protest slogans.

turns.query: Did the audit talk about how that kind of rhetoric actually made Jewish students feel less safe or welcome?
turns.answer: The audit definitely highlights that a big rise in antisemitic incidents happened on college campuses, especially during protests, and that these incidents often included rhetoric or actions that made Jewish students feel singled out or unwelcome. It specifically notes that campus incidents went up by 84% from the previous year, making up a larger share of all antisemitic incidents than ever before. So, while the audit doesn't go into personal stories or feelings, it makes it clear that this kind of rhetoric and activity is making Jewish students feel less safe and more marginalized on campus.
turns.subquestion_reasoning: Select documents that explicitly discuss the ADL's 2024 audit findings on protest-related antisemitic rhetoric and its effects on Jewish inclusion or safety; avoid sources lacking protest context or focusing solely on unrelated antisemitic incidents.
