original_query: What happens if a current or former US president attempts to stand for a third term The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution states that: No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice There are currently four living former Presidents who have been elected twice and could therefore attempt to breach this limit (Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump). What would happen if they attempted to do this, in terms of stopping them and punishing them? Would they be stopped: When they stand for election as their party's nominee in an open primary. When they are chosen as their party's nominee. When they apply to appear on the ballot paper. When they are elected. The amendment seems to only bar election, rather than standing for election, and a candidate could fail at any point before the last one (e.g. if they lose the electoral college vote). Also, if someone does attempt a third term and ends up being prevented, is there any punishment for attempting to break a constitutional term-limit? I don't think anyone has ever attempted this for the Presidential election, so there may be no direct precedent, but are there examples of other term-limited offices where someone has attempted to ignore the limits (successfully or not) which would give an indication of what might happen? Just to be clear, I'm not asking how someone could get around the term-limit (there are plenty of questions discussing this), but what would happen in terms of process and punishment if they attempted to stand for election for a third time.
original_answer: As far as I can tell, it is not a crime to run for any elected office in the US as an unqualified candidate. That said, there are a huge number of roadblocks that prevent unqualified candidates from being elected and then taking office. Roadblock #1: Getting on the ballot. It is up to election officials (typically headed by a state's Secretary of State) to keep unqualified candidates off the ballot. If a candidate is not qualified (and that includes running as a third term president), said candidate should not be appearing on the ballot. Some states even require potential write-in candidates to be qualified. Roadblock #2: Ballot counters. Assuming the election officials did their job, the official ballot counters don't need to worry about excluding votes for unqualified candidates. In states that don't certify who is/is not qualified to run for an office as a write-in candidate, they might have to toss write-in votes for, example, Mickey Mouse (a favorite write-in, where allowed). Roadblock #3: The Electoral College. The Electors swear an oath to the US Constitution, which includes the 22nd Amendment. In some states it has even been made a crime to be a Faithless Elector. That sets up a quandary if the winning candidate in some state passes the first two roadblocks but is indeed unqualified. Said electors are caught between a rock and a hard place. They might be violating state law by being faithless and voting against the elected unqualified candidate, but they might be violating state law by violating the US Constitution. Roadblock #4: The US Congress. The US Congress meets in a joint session on January 6 to certify the presidential election results. One of the things they are supposed to do is to certify that the winning candidates from each state are qualified to be president.Constitution. Roadblock #5: The US Supreme Court. Suppose that somehow an unqualified presidential candidate did make it past all of the previously mentioned roadblocks and has been elected. Everyone who opposes this election will qualify as an aggrieved party; their appeals will quickly make their way to the Supreme Court. The Court's number one job is to ensure the Constitution is obeyed. Anti-roadblock #1: Side-skirt the 22nd Amendment. There is one path to being a third term president that does not require being elected three times. This would be a reenactment of Woodrow Wilson's bizarre scheme in 1916 should Wilson have not been elected to a second term. (He was narrowly reelected in the Electoral College so Wilson's bizarre scheme was never put into play.) The issue at hand back then was the very long lame duck session between the November election and the March 4 presidential transition. In case Wilson's opponent had won the election, the plan was to appoint Charles Evans Hughes (Wilson's opponent) as US Secretary of State (second in line back then) and then Wilson and Marshall resigning. The modern equivalent would be for Mike Johnson (or whoever is speaker in 2028) to resign as Speaker of the House, the House electing Donald Trump as Speaker, and then Trump and Vance resigning. That's not going to happen. Anti-roadblock #2: Repeal the 22nd Amendment. If this gets done in time, easy-peasy; there's no longer a bar on becoming a third term President. This has come up before, almost every time the US has had a two term President since FDR. However, none of those repeal proposals had any legs. Anti-roadblock #3: Repeal and replace the entire Constitution. This, too, is a highly unlikely proposition. However, it has happened in other countries, so while highly unlikely, it is possible.

turns.query: In US presidential elections, when would officials actually block a former two-term president from getting on the ballot for a third run?
turns.answer: State officials actually have the authority to block a former two-term president from getting on the ballot if their state rules say that only eligible candidates can appear. But, states don’t have to actively check if every candidate is eligible, and sometimes ineligible candidates make it onto the ballot if there aren’t clear rules or if no one challenges it. So, whether a former two-term president is blocked really depends on how a state handles ballot access and if anyone steps in to enforce the rules.

There’s a strong connection between violating term limits and things like human rights problems or democratic backsliding, so seeing what happens elsewhere probably reinforces why the US takes its own term limits seriously—even if there’s debate or attempts to change them sometimes.

Q: In US presidential elections, when would officials actually block a former two-term president from getting on the ballot for a third run?
A: State officials actually have the authority to block a former two-term president from getting on the ballot if their state rules say that only eligible candidates can appear. But, states don’t have to actively check if every candidate is eligible, and sometimes ineligible candidates make it onto the ballot if there aren’t clear rules or if no one challenges it. So, whether a former two-term president is blocked really depends on how a state handles ballot access and if anyone steps in to enforce the rules.
Q: What if the electors just go ahead and vote for someone who’s not allowed—does anything actually happen to them?
A: If electors vote for someone who isn’t actually allowed to be president, like a former two-term president, there aren’t automatic rules that force states to check or stop those votes ahead of time. States mainly have the authority to keep ineligible candidates off the ballot, but if someone still gets votes, it really depends on whether anyone challenges it and how the state handles those situations. There isn’t a built-in system that punishes electors or automatically cancels those votes—it’s more about what the state decides to do if the issue comes up.
Q: Has Congress ever actually tried to get rid of the 22nd Amendment because of something like this?
A: Yeah, Congress has actually tried to get rid of the 22nd Amendment before, but those attempts haven’t been successful. Since the amendment was added in 1951, there have been a few efforts to repeal it, but none of them have worked out. So, the two-term limit for presidents is still firmly in place.
Q: Would courts ever actually step in on their own to stop someone from running again, or does someone have to sue first?
A: Courts don’t just step in on their own to stop someone from running again—someone usually has to bring a challenge or lawsuit first. States aren’t required to check every candidate’s eligibility, so unless there’s a specific rule or someone points out the issue, an ineligible candidate could still end up on the ballot.

turns.query: If it actually got that far, how quickly would the Supreme Court have to make a call on it?
turns.answer: There haven’t really been court cases about the 22nd Amendment’s two-term limit, so there isn’t a set timeline for how fast the Supreme Court would need to act. What we do know is that the amendment’s language is clear about not allowing someone to be elected president more than twice, and past attempts to get around that haven’t worked. So, if something did reach the Supreme Court, they’d be dealing with pretty straightforward wording, but there isn’t a history of how quickly they’d have to decide.

original_query: Which Lebanese politicians, in the 2023-24 violence cycle, had called upon Hezbollah not to persist in attacking Israel from Lebanese soil? Pretty much what the title says. One can be shocked at the numbers of deaths in Lebanon, reported to be nearly 500 two days ago , and still note that Israeli towns have been been getting targeted for almost a year and that 60000 people had to be evacuated . Many countries would not put up with that indefinitely - and Israel is not known for its pusillanimity and infinite patience, not even under less controversial war leadership than Netanyahu's - and the Lebanese establishment must have known Hezbollah was eventually going to provoke an escalated response. Since Hezbollah is not running Lebanon, and since it is drawn only from the Shiite components of Lebanese society, have non-Hezbollah/non-Shiite Lebanese politicians called on it to stand back/stand down? I am mostly interested in statements before the last two weeks, as attacks from other countries are known to have a rallying effect in most case. On the other hand, I know that in the more distant past, politicians had stated Lebanon was not ready for another war. This Q really is more about the last 6 months or so, as violence persisted. To put it another way: it is one thing to muse in the abstract about the undesirability of Hezbollah starting another war, before Hezbollah is shooting. It is another to call on Hezbollah to stop shooting when it has started to do so. Gaza is another question entirely. The rights, and wrongs, of Israeli actions in Gaza are not the rights, and wrongs, of Israeli action against Hezbollah. It is also not about the rights and wrongs of Israeli treatment of the Palestinians. Neither is this question supporting, or criticizing, the methods used by Israel to strike at Hezbollah, as of the time it was asked. This question is exclusively asking about what Lebanese politicians said about the wisdom, to Lebanese interests , of attacking Israel. If those politicians base their arguments on Gaza and/or Palestinians, sure, that is in the scope of the question. see also: ethnic/religious demographics of Lebanon in 2022
original_answer: TLDR: I'm not a regular observer of Lebanese politics, but it seems to me by surveying the statements of a few most notorious politicians there that except Christian leaders everyone else's (Sunni, Druze, not-officially-Hezbollah Shia) is either turning a blind [rhetorical] eye to Hezbollah's doings and just blaming Israel for everything, and/or actively endorsing Hezbollah's "unified arena" vision of the conflict. At least some Christian parties (not a negligible entity in Lebanon) have called for moves that are more or less similar to the US plan . May 1, 2024. The leader of a main Christian political party in Lebanon blasted the Shiite militant group Hezbollah for opening a front with Israel to back up its ally Hamas, saying it has harmed Lebanon without making a dent in Israel’s crushing offensive in the Gaza Strip. In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday night, Samir Geagea of the Lebanese Forces Party said Hezbollah should withdraw from areas along the border with Israel and the Lebanese army should deploy in all points where militants of the Iran-backed group have taken positions. [...] “All the damage that could have happened in Gaza ... happened. What was the benefit of military operations that were launched from south Lebanon? Nothing,” Geagea said, pointing the the death toll and massive destruction in Lebanon’s border villages. Not coincidentally, Christians in Lebanon have the highest level of faith in the US. Even the leader of the FPM, which is a Christian party that was traditionally allied with Hezbollah, advanced some criticism (sometime around March): "The main problem that arose recently was crossing the limits of defending Lebanon and getting involved in a conflict in which we cannot make decisions," FPM head Gebran Bassil said. Nonetheless, at about the same time Bassil was making ouvertures to Hezbollah, for a renewed political alliance, but also blaming Hezbollah for the fracture: According to him, it was Hezbollah that "left the agreement when it abandoned the principle of state-building, the partnership with the FPM, and broke the ceiling of protecting Lebanon." But words (especially from an opposition party) don't stop missiles. And the Lebanese Armed forces, which enjoy a high level of popularity in Lebanon (see previous link) have done nothing. The present central government is more affiliated with Syria, IIRC. (Sunni) PM Mikati has been quite more vague on this, e.g. 24 October 2023 Mikati paid a surprise trip to southern Lebanon on Tuesday, as Israel and the terror group — a key Hamas ally — continued to trade deadly cross-border fire, while Israel and its Western allies have repeatedly warned the group against an escalation. [...] During his visit, the caretaker prime minister emphasized what he said was Lebanon’s commitment to UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 Second Lebanon War. That resolution called for the demilitarization in southern Lebanon of all groups other than state security forces. [...] “We came to the beloved south… to reaffirm peace-loving Lebanon’s respect for all legitimate international resolutions and its commitment to implementing” resolution 1701, Mikati said, according to a statement. So, yeah, words about commitment to UN stuff. OTOH he's used far stronger terms in denouncing Israel: “The continuing Israeli aggression on Lebanon is a war of extermination in every sense of the word and a destructive plan that aims to destroy Lebanese villages and towns,” Mikati told a cabinet meeting. He urged “the United Nations and the General Assembly and influential countries... to deter the (Israeli) aggression.” Likewise, words about the "resistance doing its duty" that can easily be interpreted as moral support for Hezbollah. “We are always advocates of peace, and our choice is the choice of peace and the implementation of UN Resolution 1701. It is incumbent upon Israel to cease its repeated attacks on Lebanon and halt the war in Gaza, with everyone adhering to UN Resolution 2735,” Mikati stated. He continued: “The resistance is doing its duty, and the Lebanese government is doing its duty, and our goal is to protect the country in every sense of the word.” As another Christian politician (Samy Gemayel) put it though, as long as the Sunnis don't take a stronger stance against Hezbollah, any concrete [Lebanese] efforts against it are likely to turn into sectarian warfare. (And even if the Sunnis did take a stronger rhetorical stance, it's IMHO not a given that Hezbollah can be convinced by words, but we don't really know unless/until that happens.) Alas the Druze in Lebanon (or at least their most famous politicians) don't seem too inclined to blame Hezbollah for anything, e.g. in late July: Lebanese Druze leader Walid Jumblatt warned Saturday about Israel’s efforts to “incite strife” in the region after it accused Hezbollah of being involved in the shelling of the town of Druze in Majdal Shams in the occupied Golan Heights. Jumblatt said in light of Hezbollah’s statement denying any involvement in the attack on Druze, “We reiterate our warning and alertness to what the Israeli enemy has long been working on—to incite strife, fragment the region, and target its components,” as reported by Lebanon’s National News Agency. “We have previously thwarted this (Israeli) scheme, and now that it has reemerged, we remain vigilant alongside the resistance and all fighters confronting Israeli aggression and occupation.” And about the situation in general, he said : The armistice agreement dictates that Lebanon and Israel have a certain neutral distance in northern Lebanon as well as Palestine. But implementing the armistice agreement from one side is not logical. That's pretty close to endorsing Nasrallah's "unity of the arenas" . As for the officially-not-Hezbollah, but still Shiite politicians, like the the Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri--don't look for any calls for Hezbollah to disengage there. He was recently (August) praising the wise plans of revenge of the Iran axis, with talk like "revenge is a dish best served cold" etc. He struck a more conciliatory tone recently, after Israel struck back on a large scale. Or look at his earlier (April) interview in a London paper blaming (just) "Israeli aggression" for "turning most villages and towns situated south of the Litani river into dilapidated and uninhabitable areas" with no mention of any Hezbollah activities.

The Vicipéid article for dearg le fearg ( red with anger ) discusses the symbol: Tá ‘an fuilghrúpa O’ ar an gcúigiú straoiseog is mó úsáid i measc na nGael ar Twitter. Ní cúrsaí fola ná leighis a bhíonn i gceist ag lucht labhartha na Gaeilge nuair a bhíonn an straoiseog seo in úsáid acu, ainneoin teideal oifigiúil na siombaile, ach ‘Dearg le Fearg’. Tá an ciorcal bán ar chúlra dearg tarraingthe ag lucht an fheachtais chucu féin mar shuaitheantas idirlín. Tá leaganacha eile den chomhartha, mar shampla, ‘an ciorcal mór dearg’ ⭕, ann freisin. Roughly translated... The 'bloodgroup O' is the fifth most used emoticon amongst the Irish [speakers?] on Twitter. It's not affairs of blood or health that the Irish speaking people are talking about when they are using this emoticon, notwithstanding the official title of the symbol, but 'Red with Anger'. The white circle is drawn on a red background by the campaigners as their own internet logo. There are other versions of the sign, for example, 'the big red circle' ⭕, also. But this doesn't provide any information about it's meaning other than that it is not about blood type. And the source linked is a little more explicit: Beidh áthas ar An Dream Dearg ó thuaidh go bhfuil ‘an fuilghrúpa O’ ?ar an gcúigiú straoiseog is mó úsáid i measc na nGael ar Twitter. Ní cúrsaí fola ná leighis a bhíonn i gceist ag lucht labhartha na Gaeilge nuair a bhíonn an straoiseog seo in úsáid acu, ainneoin teideal oifigiúil na siombaile, ach an feachtas ‘Dearg le Fearg’. Tá an ciorcal bán ar chúlra dearg tarraingthe ag lucht an fheachtais chucu féin mar shuaitheantas idirlín. Roughly translated (kind of the same thing really)... An Dream Dearg from the north will be happy that 'the bloodgroup O' is the fifth most used emoticon amongst the Irish [speakers?] on Twitter. It's not affairs of blood or health that the Irish speaking people are talking about when they are using this emoticon, notwithstanding the official title of the symbol, but 'Red with Anger'. The white circle is drawn on a red background by the campaigners as their own internet logo. It is used by an dream dearg and dearg le fearg and it's not about blood type. I can't find anything concretely explaining why this symbol was chosen or what it means. The fact that it's red seems to do with anger over the failure to keep the promises of comhaontú chill rímhinn with regards to the Irish language. But that's mostly inferrence and doesn't explain much further. What is the origin and meaning of this flag?
original_answer: According to the Irish language activist Pádraig Ó Tiarnaigh, quoted in 2017 , The logo that is being shared represents An Fáinne – a circular symbol traditionally worn as a pin to show you speak, or are learning Irish. In this case we used a red background to represent anger; anger at what has occurred in recent weeks in regards to funding cuts to Líofa, and also anger at the ongoing discrimination against Irish speakers here. Líofa , which is a officially supported initiative in Northern Ireland for encouraging fluency in the language, also uses the ring symbol - in their case, a gold one. The word "fáinne" (ring) refers both to the badges and to the original language societies formed from about 1916. The founders were dissatisfied with the language policies of Sinn Féin and encouraged a stronger line, for example by asking followers to speak only Irish when interacting with British officials. The name of the society is credited to one of its founders, Colm Ó Murchadha (1889-1939), and the idea of a physical ring emblem to his compatriot Tadhg Ó Scanaill (1883-1967). (See the latter's entry at ainm.ie, citing a 1922 article in the serial Iris an Fháinne .) In the original conception, a gold ring would be awarded to people who were able to use the language to a high standard. Popularity of the rings, and the nature of organizations offering them, has ebbed and flowed; there have been several revivals of the idea. The Wikipedia page Fáinne has more detail.

original_query: How can judicial independence be jeopardised by politicians' criticism? A New Zealand minister recently called a High Court judge a "Communist Judge". Today the Bar Association published their concerns about it. They say: The judiciary in New Zealand can be an easy target. Judges cannot speak in defence of themselves or their judgments. The careful separation and balance of powers between our courts, government and politicians means Ministers must not engage in any personal criticism of judges or the leadership of the Courts. Just as the courts and judges, remain outside of politics. ... It is fundamental for our democracy that judges are not the subject of personal attack or criticism by Ministers that may risk Judges being restricted in their role. Judges must be capable of being able to freely play their independent constitutional role in Aotearoa New Zealand. This question is about how technically someone's criticism (even from a minister) can possibly adversely affect a judge's independence. Judges are not supposed to care what anyone thinks of their decisions. Indeed, being able to bring an impartial, uninfluenced mind is essential part of their job. To be independent, they are paid top notch salaries , are provided with posh perks and are legally immune from civil claims arising out of their decisions. Needless to say, they are not legally bound to anyhow react to whatever remarks politicians make about them. Their decisions do not lose legal power just because some politicians disagree. The only way politicians can legally affect judges' decisions is to enact new legislation. So, just why politicians' criticism is not water off a duck's back to judges? How can they lose their independence just because some politician says something unfavorable about them? Why wouldn't they just ignore and keep doing their job? Is that because some judges can not, despite all the legal protections, make the mental effort needed to completely ignore what powerful figures say about them? But, does this not essentially mean that these judges are not fit for the job precisely because of their inability to ignore?
original_answer: In New Zealand and broadly similar countries (in terms of socioeconomic systems) the judiciary is in principle independent of politics and interprets the law without fear or favour ( judicial independence ). This is fundamental to the rule of law , which along with (again broadly speaking) democracy underpins these societies. A politician accusing a judge of being a "communist judge" would lead some people to believe the judge's decision was biased by his communist beliefs. One politician doing this once may not be significant but the more people who do it, and the more it happens, the more likely it will become a social norm. Over time, this personal criticism will tend to erode the legitimacy of the institution of the judiciary in the eyes of the public. Unless the judiciary begins to deliver important judgements according to the prevailing wind. We have seen similar behaviour in the UK, eg. the Daily Mail's front page in November 2016 with the headline "Enemies of the people", accompanied by photos of three senior High Court judges (and their house prices) and a scathing article because the judges handed down a judgment contrary to what the Daily Mail, its owners and its readership preferred, and similar personal hostility seeping into declarations made by Government ministers and other polticians. Instead of criticising the judgment on its own merits or promoting a constructive way forward, numerous critics accused the out-of-touch, unelected (a pejorative) judges, members of a social elite who live in expensive houses, of colluding with Remainers and unscrupulous lawyers to thwart the will of the people in a shocking display of judicial activism. This has happened time and again in relation to other sets of circumstances - personal and hostile attacks on the judge instead of substantive legal criticism of the judgment and proposals of changes to the law. It is impossible to measure the consequences. Nevertheless, newspaper articles and letters and social media comments show there are people who seem to believe that a judgment that one disagrees with is proof of the judge's bias. Often we don't know what we've got until it's gone . None of us are old enough to remember the time when English Kings and Queens dismissed senior judges for disagreeable judgments. But there are countries today where judicial independence is said to be at risk (e.g. Poland and Hungary) and there are other countries where there hasn't been judicial independence. These don't tend to be places where people are eager to live, rather than to leave, if you are on the 'wrong' side.

turns.query: In judicial independence, how can constant public criticism from politicians actually end up making it harder for judges to stay impartial?
turns.answer: Constant public criticism from politicians can actually make it harder for judges to stay impartial because it creates pressure for judges to make decisions that will please those in power, rather than just following the law. Judges who want to move up in their careers might start worrying about how their rulings will be seen by politicians or influential people, and that can make it tempting to rule in a way that lines up with political opinions instead of being truly neutral.

original_query: How does the Israeli administration of the Golan Heights affect its current non-Jewish population? Two-thirds of the Golan Heights - 1200/1800 sq km have been controlled by Israel. There are 25000 Arabs (nearly all Druze) as well as about 25000 Israelis living there. There is a lot of media coverage, concerning the situations for Palestinians in the West Bank, within Israel proper and within Gaza. Some will even point out the differences between area A and area C administration in the West Bank. Depending on one's viewpoint, the situation for Palestinians will be described as either "catastrophic", or the "best Israel can do". Either way, there is no lack of information about Israeli administration. In contrast, we hear very little media coverage about the Golan Heights. How does the Israeli control and administration, concerning non-Jewish residents, compare to say that of the West Bank? My understanding, among other things, is that Druze can apply for Israeli citizenship if they choose to. After the recent Hezbullah strike that left 12 children dead , media coverage didn't seem very clear about locals' sentiments and perception of Israel. p.s. This is request for information about an area that we hear little about. No more, no less. The international community in general does not recognize the annexation of the Golan, but it is also not difficult to understand the military rationale for occupying high ground of such strategic value when it belongs to Syria, a state Israeli is still technically at war with. So this question is not supporting, or objecting to, Israeli control, merely asking how residents are affected. p.p.s. I also understand that in 1967 a larger population of Syrian Arabs either fled the area, was evacuated or was chased out. This question is only asking about the effect on those who stayed behind.
original_answer: Nobody likes getting hit with missiles, so discussing that is a bit too obvious. The Times of Israel has a long piece discussing the feeling/attitudes of the Druze in the Golan vs other parts of north Israel. My TLDR summary: the Druze in the Golan were slower to warm up to Israeli citizenship, and some still dig Assad, but after the civil war in Syria hardly any Golan Druze use the perks that Assad allows for them, e.g. free higher education (in Syria) etc. OTOH, they [the Golan Druze] still mostly shun Israeli elections.

turns.query: In the Golan Heights, why have many Druze residents been hesitant to apply for Israeli citizenship since Israel took control?
turns.answer: Many Druze residents in the Golan Heights have been hesitant to apply for Israeli citizenship for a few reasons. A lot of them still identify as Syrian and worry about what might happen if the area is ever returned to Syrian control, especially since they have relatives in Syria or fear being mistreated by Syrian authorities. There's also been a history of social pressure within the community, making it controversial or even secretive to take Israeli citizenship, even though their standard of living in Israel is higher and they have access to social benefits.
